heading: EverMind
sub: Every knowledge base only knows what somebody thought to write down.
narration: Every support team has a knowledge base. And every knowledge base has the same quiet problem: it only knows what somebody thought to write down. Whatever it was never told, it simply can't answer — no matter how many times the question comes in.

heading: The Cost of Forgetting
lines: Next week, somebody asks it again.
narration: Here's what actually happens today. Someone answers the question by hand, from memory, under deadline. It's never written down anywhere the system can use. So next week, a different customer asks the exact same thing — and somebody answers it by hand again. Twenty minutes, every repeat, forever.

heading: This Is EverMind
lines: Reads what the knowledge base missed.
A person reviews a decision — not a pile of raw questions.
narration: This is EverMind. It reads the log of questions your knowledge base couldn't answer, and does the first pass on every one of them — so a person sitting down to review ends up looking at a short list of decisions, not a long list of raw, unsorted questions.

heading: The Whole Idea, In One Picture

flow.label: Draft, with source
flow.sub: cites a real document, or declines

flow.label: Human approves
flow.sub: the only way anything moves forward

flow.label: Knowledge base
flow.sub: unchanged until a person says so

narration: Here's the whole idea in one picture. Questions come in from the log. Similar ones get grouped together, so five people asking the same thing in five different ways becomes one decision, not five. Every group gets sorted into one of three outcomes. A genuine gap gets drafted with a source attached. And the only way anything crosses into your knowledge base is a person, on the right, signing off.

heading: Outcome One: A Genuine Gap

boxes.title: “If I ship DDP, who gets the duty bill?”
boxes.sub: a real question from the log

boxes.title: “The shipper is billed for duty, tax and handling.”
boxes.sub: drafted, citing the duty and tax guide

narration: This question had never been answered before. EverMind found it, checked the trusted source documents, and drafted an answer — with the exact document it came from attached, so a reviewer can verify it in seconds instead of researching it from scratch.

heading: Outcome Two: Already Answered

boxes.title: “International shipping — how long?”
boxes.sub: a different phrasing of an existing entry

boxes.title: Matched to an existing answer
boxes.sub: no draft written — nothing new needed

narration: This one only looks new. It's the same question your knowledge base already answers, just worded differently. EverMind recognizes the match and stops there — no wasted drafting, and no duplicate entry cluttering the knowledge base for your team to clean up later.

heading: Outcome Three: Not Ours to Answer

boxes.title: “Any jobs going at the Amsterdam depot?”
boxes.sub: a real question from the log

boxes.title: Declined — unrelated to the knowledge base

narration: And some questions simply aren't support questions at all. This one's about a job opening, not a shipment. EverMind recognizes that too, and declines before it ever gets near drafting — it knows the difference between a gap in the knowledge base and a question that was never its job to answer.

heading: Before We Wrote Any Code
narration: Before writing a line of code, we wrote down exactly what this system must do — and just as importantly, what it must never do — and had that reviewed before the build even started. Same discipline any engineering organization uses before committing real resources: agree the requirements in writing, then build to them, not the other way around.

heading: Checked Against Known Answers
lines: Real questions, with the right answer already known.
Every outcome checked — gaps, duplicates, and the ones to decline.
Not “does this look reasonable,” but “did it get the right answer.”
narration: Before we'd trust this on anything real, we tested it against questions where we already know the correct outcome — fifty-nine of them, covering genuine gaps, duplicates, and questions it should refuse. That turns the question from ‘does this look reasonable’ into ‘did it get the right answer,’ which is a much higher bar, and the one that actually matters.

heading: What a Reviewed Decision Looks Like in Code
sub: Every answer carries its source, its confidence, and a reason — or it doesn't get created at all.
narration: Here's what that discipline looks like in the actual code. Every answer the system drafts has to carry its source, a confidence score, and a stated reason — or the object simply can't be created. This isn't a guideline we hope gets followed. It's enforced in the data structure itself, before a draft can exist at all.

heading: What Comes Out the Other Side
sub: One reviewable decision per gap, ready to check in under a minute.
narration: And this is what comes out the other side after a run. One reviewable decision per gap, the source right there next to the answer, ready for a person to check in under a minute — instead of researching and writing it from nothing.

heading: The Part That Matters Most
lines: Not automatically. Not under any setting.
narration: Here's the part that matters most, and the part worth remembering above everything else in this video: EverMind never publishes anything. Not once. Not automatically, and not under any configuration or setting you could turn on. There is no version of this where it skips the human.

heading: There's No Path That Lets It

boxes.title: EverMind writes
boxes.sub: one file — the draft queue. Nothing else.

boxes.title: A person writes
boxes.sub: the knowledge base. The only writer there is.

narration: And it isn't a policy we're asking you to trust on good faith. There's no path in the code that lets it happen. The only thing the system is capable of writing is one list, for a person to read. Reaching your actual knowledge base from there requires a separate, deliberate, human action — every single time.

heading: It Treats Every Question as Data
lines: A question is text to read.
Even if someone tries to make it one.
narration: One more trust point, because this question always comes up: what if someone tries to manipulate it? Every logged question is treated strictly as text to read — never as an instruction the system follows. If someone embeds a command inside a question, the worst case is a rejected draft a human discards in seconds. There's no path from a clever question to an unreviewed action.

heading: A Person Decides
narration: So here's how it actually reaches a customer. A person reads the drafted decision, checks the cited source themselves, and decides whether to approve it. That's the only way anything this system finds ever reaches the knowledge base, and from there, a customer.

heading: The Scale

boxes.title: Every month, every team
boxes.sub: any support organization with a knowledge base has this exact gap

narration: Fifty-nine questions, one team, one month. That's not a one-time cleanup — it repeats every month, and it repeats on every team you have that runs a knowledge base. The twenty-minute tax from the start of this video isn't an incident. It's the ongoing cost of doing nothing.

heading: The Honest Limit

boxes.title: No source, no answer
boxes.sub: when it can't find real evidence, it says so

boxes.title: It doesn't guess
boxes.sub: an unsupported draft is treated as invalid, not weak

narration: And we want to be upfront about its limit, because every tool that sounds this capable eventually gets asked to do more than it should. When EverMind can't find a real source to support an answer, it says so. It doesn't guess, and it doesn't fill the gap with something plausible. An answer with no evidence behind it isn't treated as a weak answer — it's treated as an invalid one, and it never reaches a reviewer at all.

heading: That's EverMind.
sub: Built from real questions. Tested against known answers. Ready for one real knowledge base.
narration: This is a working project, built from real support questions, with every decision it makes already defined and already tested against known answers — not a concept on a slide. We're not asking you to change how your team works today. We're asking for the chance to run this against one real knowledge base, and show you the twenty minutes back. That's EverMind.
